lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A game stream can report a perfectly healthy bitrate and still feel late. So what's actually going on?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I'd guess the network. It's always the network.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Not always. Antoine's project, Artemis Switch, is his fork of Moonlight-Switch for the Nintendo Switch, and it focuses on one thing: the path between receiving a frame and putting it on screen. The question isn't how fast the decoder is. It's where each frame waited.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Okay, so what does the pipeline look like?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A PC host, Sunshine or Apollo, sends video over the Moonlight protocol. The Switch decodes it with FFmpeg and NVDEC, drops it in a queue, picks a frame, and presents it with deko3d. And that split matters. A wrong virtual display mode is a host problem. A decoded-frame queue that keeps growing is a client problem.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That's a handy way to know who to blame.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It is. Now here's the subtle part. When the queue has a backlog, the code throws away old frames to favor freshness. But it checks the oldest frame's deadline first, before jumping to the newest one.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Picture a bouncer who resets the wait time every time someone new walks in. If the gate follows the newest frame, its deadline keeps moving forward. Frames keep arriving, but nothing ever gets shown. Keeping the oldest deadline avoids that starvation.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Huh. That's a tiny rule with a big effect.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: And there's a telemetry class that measures each stage separately: decode time, queue wait, render cost, GPU submission, real video bitrate. Antoine is careful about what it covers, though. The client pipeline starts after the network finishes. It doesn't include host encoding, display scanout or controller delay.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: No. His advice for testing on hardware is to keep the host, scene, resolution and network fixed, change one pacing option at a time, and test handheld and docked separately. A lower average with worse spikes can feel worse.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And compiling isn't the same as playing well, I assume.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. The README itself separates portable tests and release builds from real device validation. The takeaway: measure where the frame waits, not just how fast things decode. The full write-up has the pipeline diagram and links to the two source files.
